guide.summary: The Ancient Mediterranean unit (36 works, about 15% of the exam) spans the Near East, Egypt, Greece, Etruria, and Rome. It tracks how rulers used art for power, how cultures prepared for the afterlife, how the human figure moved from conceptual to naturalistic, and how architecture evolved from mud brick to Roman concrete domes.

sections.heading: Overview: three traditions, one sea
sections.body:
Unit 2 has **36 required works** and about **15% of the exam**. It covers the Ancient Near East (Sumer, Babylon, Assyria, Persia), Egypt, and the Greek, Etruscan, and Roman worlds. These cultures traded and fought with one another, so the most-tested ideas are **exchange and adaptation**: Egyptian standing figures shaping the Greek kouros, Greek temples shaping Etruscan and Roman temples, Greek sculpture copied and reworked by Romans.

Common themes to have ready for essays:
- **Art and power**: rulers shown through hierarchical scale, divine connection, and idealized bodies (Narmer, Hammurabi, Lamassu, Persepolis, Augustus).
- **Art and the afterlife**: tombs, coffins, funerary texts, and grave markers (pyramids, Tutankhamun, Hunefer, Anavysos Kouros, Hegeso, Etruscan tombs).
- **The human figure**: the move from conceptual, frontal figures to naturalism, contrapposto, and then Hellenistic emotion and Roman verism.
- **Architecture and engineering**: mud-brick ziggurats, post-and-lintel stone temples, Greek orders, Roman concrete, arches, and domes.

sections.heading: Ancient Near East
sections.body:
**White Temple and its ziggurat** (Uruk, modern Warka, Iraq, Sumerian, c. 3500–3000 BCE, mud brick): a temple, probably to the sky god Anu, raised on a stepped mud-brick platform. Height brought the shrine closer to the gods; the whitewashed surface made it shine; an indirect, bent-axis approach slowed the climb. Only priests entered the shrine.

**Statues of votive figures** (Square Temple at Eshnunna, modern Tell Asmar, Iraq, Sumerian, c. 2700 BCE, gypsum inlaid with shell and black limestone): worshippers with huge inlaid eyes and clasped hands, placed in the temple to **pray perpetually** on behalf of donors. Size differences may reflect status.

**Standard of Ur** (Royal Tombs at Ur, modern Tell el-Muqayyar, Iraq, Sumerian, c. 2600–2400 BCE, wood inlaid with shell, lapis lazuli, and red limestone): a hollow box with a "War" side and a "Peace" side, each in three **registers** read bottom to top. The king is larger (**hierarchical scale**), breaking the frame on top. Imported lapis (from Afghanistan) shows long-distance trade. Its original function is unknown (a standard, soundbox, or box).

**Code of Hammurabi** (Babylon; found at Susa, modern Iran; c. 1792–1750 BCE, basalt): a stele with Hammurabi standing before the seated sun god **Shamash**, god of justice, who has flames rising from his shoulders and offers a rod and ring of authority. Below are 282 laws in cuneiform (Akkadian). Image + text tell viewers the laws are divinely sanctioned. Shamash's shoulders are frontal while his head is in profile (composite view). Elamites later carried it to Susa as war booty.

**Lamassu** (citadel of Sargon II, Dur Sharrukin, modern Khorsabad, Iraq, Neo-Assyrian, c. 720–705 BCE, alabaster): human-headed winged bulls guarding gateways. They have **five legs**, so they look complete from the front (standing) and side (striding). They combine high relief and sculpture in the round, and their horned caps signal divinity—apotropaic (protective) and intimidating to visitors.

**Audience Hall (apadana) of Darius and Xerxes** (Persepolis, Iran, Persian, c. 520–465 BCE, limestone): a vast hypostyle hall (originally 72 columns, few still standing) with **double-bull capitals**. Staircase reliefs show delegations from subject peoples bringing tribute in orderly procession—an image of a multiethnic empire held together by the king. The Persians absorbed forms from Egypt, Assyria, and Greece (Ionian stonemasons worked there).

sections.heading: Egypt: permanence, order, and afterlife
sections.body:
Egyptian art preserved **ma'at** (cosmic order) through conventions held steady for 3,000 years: composite view, registers, hierarchical scale, and stiff frontal poses for rulers.

- **Palette of King Narmer** (Predynastic, c. 3000–2920 BCE, greywacke): ceremonial palette commemorating the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. Narmer wears the **white crown of Upper Egypt** on one side (smiting an enemy) and the **red crown of Lower Egypt** on the other (reviewing beheaded enemies). Intertwined serpopards form the circle where cosmetics would have been ground. Registers, ground lines, composite view, and hierarchical scale all appear here first.
- **Seated scribe** (Saqqara, Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, c. 2620–2500 BCE, painted limestone): a non-royal official shown with realistic sagging flesh and inlaid crystal eyes—more naturalistic than royal images, because he is not bound by royal idealization.
- **Great Pyramids (Menkaura, Khafre, Khufu) and Great Sphinx** (Giza, Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, c. 2550–2490 BCE, cut limestone): royal tombs in a complex with mortuary and valley temples; Khufu's is largest. The pyramid shape may evoke the sun's rays or the primordial mound. The Sphinx likely bears Khafre's face on a lion's body.
- **King Menkaura and queen** (Old Kingdom, 4th Dynasty, c. 2490–2472 BCE, greywacke): frontal, rigid, left foot forward, fists clenched, attached to a back slab; the queen embraces him. Durable stone and closed form express eternity; it was a **ka** statue for his valley temple. It is unfinished at the bottom.
- **Temple of Amun-Re and Hypostyle Hall** (Karnak, near Luxor, New Kingdom, 18th and 19th Dynasties; temple c. 1550 BCE, hall c. 1250 BCE; cut sandstone and mud brick): 134 massive papyrus columns, a **clerestory** admitting light, and spaces growing darker and more restricted toward the sanctuary—only priests and the pharaoh went deepest.
- **Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut** (near Luxor, New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1473–1458 BCE; sandstone partially carved into a rock cliff, red granite): three colonnaded terraces set against the cliffs at Deir el-Bahri. Hatshepsut, a female pharaoh, was depicted with male regalia including the false beard; reliefs record her trade expedition to Punt.
- **Akhenaten, Nefertiti, and three daughters** (New Kingdom, Amarna, 18th Dynasty, c. 1353–1335 BCE, limestone): a house-altar relief in **sunken relief**. Under the Aten sun disk, whose rays end in hands holding ankhs, the royal family relaxes intimately, with elongated heads and soft bellies—a deliberate break tied to Akhenaten's **monotheistic** worship of Aten.
- **Tutankhamun's tomb, innermost coffin** (New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1323 BCE, gold with inlay of enamel and semiprecious stones): the king as Osiris with crook and flail and the nemes headdress; vulture (Nekhbet) and cobra (Wadjet) on his brow; protective wings of goddesses. Return to tradition after Amarna. Found by Howard Carter in 1922.
- **Last judgment of Hunefer** (page from the Book of the Dead, New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, c. 1275 BCE, painted papyrus scroll): Anubis leads Hunefer and weighs his heart against the **feather of Ma'at**; Ammit waits to devour a failed heart; Thoth records; Horus presents Hunefer to enthroned Osiris. Read left to right, top register shows him before gods.

sections.heading: Greece: from Archaic to Hellenistic
sections.body:
**Archaic (c. 600–480 BCE)**: The **Anavysos Kouros** (c. 530 BCE, marble with remnants of paint) adapts the Egyptian stance (left foot forward, arms at sides) but is nude and freestanding; the **Archaic smile** and stylized hair are typical. It marked the grave of Kroisos, a young man killed in battle, as the inscription says. The **Peplos Kore** (Acropolis, c. 530 BCE, marble, painted details) was a votive on the Acropolis; drill holes suggest she once held attributes, so she may represent a goddess rather than a maiden. Traces of paint remind us Greek sculpture was colored.

**Classical (c. 480–323 BCE)**: Polykleitos' **Doryphoros** (original 450–440 BCE; Roman marble copy of a bronze original) demonstrates his **Canon** of ideal proportions and **contrapposto**, a weight shift with balanced tense and relaxed limbs (chiastic balance). The **Acropolis** (Athens, Iktinos and Kallikrates, c. 447–410 BCE, marble) was rebuilt under Pericles after the Persians sacked it, partly with **Delian League** funds. The **Parthenon** is a Doric temple with an Ionic continuous frieze (the Panathenaic procession), refined by optical corrections (column swelling or entasis, upward-curving stylobate); Phidias oversaw the sculpture, including the gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos. Also: the **Erechtheion** with its caryatid porch, the **Temple of Athena Nike** with the "Nike adjusting her sandal" parapet relief in clinging drapery, and the **Propylaia** gateway. The **Niobides Krater** (Niobid Painter, c. 460–450 BCE, clay, red-figure with white highlights) shows Apollo and Artemis killing Niobe's children, with figures placed on **multiple ground lines**—an early attempt at spatial depth, probably reflecting lost wall painting. The **Grave stele of Hegeso** (attributed to Kallimachos, c. 410 BCE, marble and paint) shows a seated woman choosing jewelry (once painted) from a box held by a servant—an image of her domestic role and family wealth.

**Hellenistic (323–31 BCE)**: drama, movement, and emotion. The **Winged Victory of Samothrace** (c. 190 BCE, marble) lands on a ship's prow, drapery whipped by wind—likely commemorating a naval victory and originally set in a fountain. The **Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon** (c. 175 BCE, marble) wraps a high-relief **Gigantomachy** (gods vs. giants) around its base; figures spill onto the stairs; Athena seizes the giant Alkyoneus by the hair while Gaia rises in anguish—an allegory of Pergamon's victories over the Gauls. The **Seated boxer** (c. 100 BCE, bronze) is exhausted and battered, with copper inlay for blood and cauliflower ears—an anti-heroic subject.

sections.heading: Etruscans and Romans
sections.body:
**Etruscan**: The **Temple of Minerva** (Veii, c. 510–500 BCE) had a high podium, frontal stairs, deep porch, and three cellas in wood, mud brick, or tufa, with terra cotta statues on the roof ridge, including the striding **Apollo** attributed to the master sculptor **Vulca**. The **Sarcophagus of the Spouses** (c. 520 BCE, terra cotta) shows a couple reclining together at a banquet—evidence of Etruscan women's relatively high social status. The **Tomb of the Triclinium** (Tarquinia, c. 480–470 BCE, tufa and fresco) has banqueters, dancers, and musicians, a celebratory funerary vision.

**Roman Republic**: The **Head of a Roman patrician** (c. 75–50 BCE, marble) is **veristic**—deep wrinkles and sunken cheeks signal age, wisdom, and *gravitas*, values of the senatorial class; it relates to ancestor masks (imagines). The **Alexander Mosaic** (House of the Faun, Pompeii, c. 100 BCE, tesserae) copies a Greek painting of Alexander defeating Darius III, with dramatic foreshortening (a horse seen from behind) and shading.

**Roman Empire**: The **Augustus of Prima Porta** (early 1st century CE, marble) borrows the Doryphoros' contrapposto and idealized face but adds an **adlocutio** (address) gesture, a cuirass showing the return of Roman standards from the Parthians, bare feet (divinity), and Cupid on a dolphin (descent from Venus). It was found at the villa of his wife Livia. The **House of the Vettii** (Pompeii, c. 2nd century BCE; rebuilt c. 62–79 CE) belonged to two wealthy freedmen; its atrium, impluvium, peristyle garden, and Fourth Style frescoes show status display. The **Colosseum** (Rome, 70–80 CE, stone and concrete), built by the Flavians on the site of Nero's private lake, stacks Tuscan, Ionic, and Corinthian engaged columns over arches, with concrete barrel and groin vaults—"bread and circuses" architecture returning land to the public. The **Forum of Trajan** (Apollodorus of Damascus; forum and markets 106–112 CE; column 113 CE) includes the Basilica Ulpia, libraries, markets, and **Trajan's Column** with a spiral frieze of the Dacian Wars. The **Pantheon** (118–125 CE, concrete with stone facing), built under Hadrian, joins a traditional temple portico to a domed rotunda with a coffered dome and an open **oculus**; the dome's diameter equals its height, so a sphere fits inside—a model of the heavens. The **Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus** (Late Imperial, c. 250 CE, marble) packs Romans and Goths into a chaotic surface with no space; a bareheaded general at the center gestures in triumph—the crowding, deep drilling, and loss of classical clarity signal change in the unstable third century.

keyTakeaways: Near East: hierarchical scale, registers, divine kingship; Lamassu and Persepolis project imperial power.
Egypt: conventions (composite view, frontality, registers) preserve order; Amarna is the one dramatic break.
Greek figure evolves: Archaic (kouros, smile) → Classical (contrapposto, Canon, idealism) → Hellenistic (emotion, movement, realism).
Romans copied Greek forms but used them for political messaging (Augustus) and developed concrete, arches, vaults, domes.
Etruscan temples: podium, frontal stairs, deep porch, terra cotta roof statues; Etruscan women shown as equals at banquets.
Know at least two works from each culture for Q1/Q2 lists.
commonMistakes: Saying the Doryphoros we see is Greek — it is a Roman marble copy of a lost Greek bronze.
Confusing Narmer's crowns: white = Upper (south) Egypt, red = Lower (north) Egypt.
Placing the Code of Hammurabi in Iraq as its find spot — it was found at Susa, Iran.
Calling the Pergamon frieze 'Classical' — it is Hellenistic.
Describing Roman veristic portraits as unflattering; verism signaled admired virtues.
Saying the Parthenon is Ionic — it is Doric with an Ionic frieze.
examTips: About 15% of the exam: expect 10–12 MCQs and possibly a long essay or continuity question.
Continuity-and-change prompts love: Egypt → kouros; Doryphoros → Augustus; Greek temple → Etruscan/Roman temple; classical clarity → Ludovisi crowding.
Contextual questions often focus on patrons (Pericles, Augustus, the Vettii brothers) and on funding (Delian League).
Attribution items show unknown Greek vases, Roman portraits, or Egyptian statues—know the style markers of each period.

vocab.definition: Showing the most important figure largest regardless of spatial logic.
vocab.example: Narmer, the king on the Standard of Ur.

vocab.definition: A horizontal band dividing a surface into zones, each with its own ground line.
Combining profile and frontal views in one figure (e.g., profile head and legs, frontal eye and shoulders).
A stepped mud-brick platform in Mesopotamia supporting a temple.
An upright carved stone slab with images and/or text.
The Egyptian life force that survives death and needs a statue or body as a home.
A large interior space whose roof rests on many rows of columns.
A raised section of wall with windows that admits light above a roof line.
Relief carved into the surface so figures sit below the surrounding plane; common in Egypt.
Archaic Greek freestanding statues of a nude young man / clothed young woman, used as grave markers or votives.
A pose with weight on one leg, creating a shift in hips and shoulders and a natural, relaxed balance.
A set of ideal proportions; Polykleitos' Canon expressed in the Doryphoros.
Greek vase technique leaving figures in the red clay color against a black-glazed background, allowing painted detail lines.
Greek orders: Doric has plain cushion capitals and no base; Ionic has volute (scroll) capitals; Corinthian has acanthus-leaf capitals.
Slight swelling of a column shaft to correct the optical illusion of thinness.
Roman Republican hyper-realism in portraiture, stressing age and experience as signs of virtue.
A gesture of a general addressing troops, used in Augustus of Prima Porta.
A round opening at the top of a dome, as in the Pantheon.
A recessed panel in a ceiling or dome that lightens weight and adds pattern.
Intended to ward off evil; e.g., Lamassu guarding a gate.
The mythic battle of the gods against the giants; used as an allegory of civilization over barbarism.

practice.stem: On the Palette of King Narmer, the king's larger size compared with the other figures is an example of

choices.text: atmospheric perspective
contrapposto
hierarchical scale
verism

practice.explanation: Importance is shown by size: Narmer towers over his enemies and attendants.

distractors.B: Contrapposto is a Greek weight-shift pose.
distractors.A: Atmospheric perspective uses haze for distance.

practice.stem: The Parthenon on the Athenian Acropolis is primarily built in which order?

choices.text: Doric
Corinthian
Tuscan
Ionic

practice.explanation: The Parthenon is a Doric temple, though it incorporates Ionic features such as the continuous interior frieze.

distractors.B: Corinthian came later and appears in Roman works like the Pantheon portico.
distractors.D: Ionic elements appear (frieze), but the colonnade is Doric.

practice.stem: The oculus of the Pantheon is

choices.text: a spiral relief band around a column
a sculpted guardian figure at the entrance
a round opening at the top of the dome
a stepped platform beneath the temple

practice.explanation: The oculus is the circular opening, about 27 feet across, at the crown of the Pantheon's dome.

distractors.D: That suggests a ziggurat or podium.

practice.stem: The Code of Hammurabi stele shows Hammurabi before Shamash. Shamash is the god of

choices.text: war
the underworld
fertility
justice and the sun

practice.explanation: Shamash, the sun god and god of justice, grants Hammurabi authority, legitimizing the laws inscribed below.

practice.stem: The relief of Akhenaten, Nefertiti, and three daughters differs from earlier Egyptian royal images chiefly because it

choices.text: shows the royal family in relaxed, intimate poses with elongated, curving bodies
depicts the king smiting enemies in battle
uses hierarchical scale for the first time
uses linear perspective to create a deep interior

practice.explanation: Amarna art broke with rigid, idealized royal convention: the family plays with the children under the Aten's rays, with elongated heads and soft bodies, reflecting Akhenaten's religious revolution.

distractors.B: Smiting scenes are traditional (Narmer), not Amarna innovations.
distractors.D: Egyptian art did not use linear perspective.
distractors.C: Hierarchical scale appears from the Narmer Palette on.

practice.stem: A marble statue of a nude young man stands rigidly frontal with his left foot forward, arms at his sides, fists clenched, and a slight smile. It was set up over a grave around 530 BCE. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: The sculptor was trained in Rome.
The figure adapts Egyptian conventions for standing figures within a Greek funerary tradition.
The statue represents an elderly senator.
The figure was originally made of bronze and later copied by Romans.

practice.explanation: This describes the Anavysos Kouros type: the striding, frontal stance derives from Egyptian figures like Menkaura, but the figure is freestanding and nude and served as a Greek grave marker.

distractors.C: Kouroi idealize youth; verism is Roman Republican.
distractors.D: Kouroi were carved in marble; the copy issue applies to the Doryphoros.
distractors.A: Rome had no such tradition in 530 BCE.

practice.stem: The Lamassu from the citadel of Sargon II was carved with five legs most likely so that it would

choices.text: appear complete and stable when viewed from the front and in motion when viewed from the side
represent two separate creatures
indicate it was an animal used in battle
balance the weight of the wings structurally

practice.explanation: From the front the figure stands firmly; from the side it strides past the viewer. The fifth leg makes both views complete—a conceptual solution suited to a gateway guardian.

distractors.C: It is a protective divine being, not a war animal.
distractors.D: The legs are carved in relief against the block, not structural supports for wings.

practice.stem: Augustus of Prima Porta draws on the Doryphoros for its pose and proportions. Which feature of the Augustus most clearly ADDS a Roman political message absent from the Greek model?

choices.text: The idealized youthful face
The cuirass showing the return of military standards from the Parthians
The use of marble
The contrapposto stance

practice.explanation: The breastplate's narrative of the Parthians returning captured standards advertises Augustus' diplomatic and military success—propaganda absent from the Doryphoros.

distractors.A: Idealization is borrowed from the Greek model.
distractors.C: The surviving Doryphoros is also marble (a Roman copy).

practice.stem: Which pairing correctly matches a Roman building with a structural innovation central to its design?

choices.text: Colosseum — post-and-lintel stone beams only
Forum of Trajan — mud-brick ziggurat
Pantheon — a concrete dome with coffers and an oculus
House of the Vettii — flying buttresses

practice.explanation: The Pantheon's unreinforced concrete dome, lightened by coffers and lighter aggregate toward the top, and the oculus, are its defining engineering features.

distractors.A: The Colosseum relies on concrete arches and vaults; columns are decorative engaged columns.

practice.stem: Which of the following best characterizes the Seated boxer compared with Classical works such as the Doryphoros?

choices.text: It presents an idealized hero at rest in perfect balance.
It shows a ruler addressing his troops.
It uses rigid frontality derived from Egypt.
It emphasizes physical damage, exhaustion, and emotion in a realistic way.

practice.explanation: The Hellenistic Seated boxer has a broken nose, cauliflower ears, copper-inlaid wounds, and a weary upward glance—realism and pathos instead of Classical idealism.

practice.stem: The Parthenon was built under Pericles partly with funds from the Delian League, an alliance formed to defend Greek city-states against Persia. Art historians use this fact most directly to argue that the Acropolis

choices.text: was a modest structure built by private donors
was designed by Persian architects
expressed Athenian imperial power as well as piety
was primarily a military fortress

practice.explanation: Diverting allied treasury money to monumental temples made the Acropolis a statement of Athens' dominance over its allies, not only devotion to Athena.

distractors.D: By this time the Acropolis was a sanctuary, not a fortress.
distractors.A: It was a state project of enormous cost.

practice.stem: The Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus is often cited as evidence of change in Roman art in the third century CE. Which visual feature best supports that claim?

choices.text: Figures arranged clearly on a single ground line with ample space between them
A narrative that unrolls in a spiral band
A calm, idealized central figure modeled on Polykleitos' Canon
A tightly packed composition that abandons clear spatial depth, with deep drilling creating strong contrasts

practice.explanation: The crowded, spaceless surface and chiaroscuro from deep drilling break from classical clarity; scholars connect this to the instability of the period (frequent wars and short reigns).

distractors.A: That is the opposite of the Ludovisi composition.
distractors.C: The central general is energetic, not a calm Canon figure.

practice.stem: An Etruscan temple and a Greek temple of the same period differ in that the Etruscan temple typically

choices.text: had no cella
was raised on a high podium with steps only at the front, emphasizing a frontal approach
was built entirely of marble with sculpture in the pediment
was surrounded on all sides by a single row of columns on a low stepped base

practice.explanation: Etruscan temples (e.g., the Temple of Minerva at Veii) had a tall podium, frontal stairs, a deep porch, and three cellas; Greek temples had a peripteral colonnade on a stepped base approachable from all sides.

distractors.C: Etruscan temples used wood, mud brick, and tufa, with terra cotta roof sculpture.
distractors.D: That describes a Greek peripteral temple.

practice.stem: An unknown limestone relief shows a royal couple with elongated skulls, narrow faces, thin necks, and protruding bellies seated beneath a disk whose rays end in small hands. The relief was most likely produced

choices.text: during the reign of Akhenaten at Amarna
in Neo-Assyrian Khorsabad for a palace gate
in Old Kingdom Egypt to decorate a pyramid temple
in Archaic Greece as a grave marker

practice.explanation: The Aten disk with hand-tipped rays and the elongated, soft body style are diagnostic of the Amarna period, as in the image-set relief of Akhenaten, Nefertiti, and three daughters.

distractors.B: Assyrian reliefs show muscular bearded figures and no Aten.
distractors.D: Greek grave markers do not use the sun disk.
distractors.C: Old Kingdom royal images are idealized and rigid (Menkaura).

practice.prompt:
The work described is Augustus of Prima Porta, Imperial Roman, early first century CE, marble. It shows Augustus standing in contrapposto, right arm raised in an address gesture, wearing a carved breastplate, with bare feet and a small Cupid riding a dolphin beside his right leg.

A. Describe ONE visual characteristic of Augustus of Prima Porta.
B. Describe ANOTHER visual characteristic of Augustus of Prima Porta.
C. Using specific visual evidence, explain how the work demonstrates continuity with Classical Greek sculpture.
D. Using specific visual evidence, explain how the work demonstrates change from Classical Greek sculpture.
E. Using specific visual or contextual evidence, explain why this change served the political purposes of Augustus.

rubric.description: Accurately describes a visual feature (contrapposto, raised arm, breastplate reliefs, bare feet, Cupid on dolphin, idealized youthful face).
Uses visual evidence to link to Greek sculpture, e.g., contrapposto and idealized proportions modeled on Polykleitos' Doryphoros.
Uses visual evidence to explain change, e.g., clothed in armor, specific portrait, adlocutio gesture, narrative breastplate, supporting Cupid.

Explains how the change served Augustus: e.g., Parthian standards on the cuirass advertise peace through victory; Cupid claims divine descent from Venus; youthful idealization denies aging and promotes a golden age.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Augustus stands with his weight on his right leg and his left leg relaxed, in contrapposto.

B. His right arm is raised in the adlocutio gesture, as if addressing troops, and he wears a cuirass carved with figures, including a Parthian handing back a Roman military standard.

C. The statue continues the Classical Greek ideal seen in Polykleitos' Doryphoros: the same weight shift and counterbalanced limbs, and an idealized, smooth, youthful face and body that follow ideal proportions rather than showing age.

D. Unlike the nude, anonymous Doryphoros, which represents an ideal athlete, Augustus is a specific, recognizable ruler, dressed in military armor, making a gesture of command toward the viewer. The cuirass turns the body into a surface for narrative, and the Cupid riding a dolphin serves as a support and a symbol.

E. These changes turned a Greek ideal of beauty into Roman propaganda. The breastplate's scene of the Parthians returning the standards lost by Crassus celebrates Augustus' diplomatic triumph and the Pax Romana, and the Cupid on a dolphin refers to Venus, the mythic ancestor of the Julian family, implying divine descent. Combining the authority of Greek perfection with these specific Roman messages presented Augustus as an ageless, divinely favored leader.
